**Seat map.** Served from Redis, refreshed every second or two from the table; a seat that looks free but is taken just fails the conditional update and the UI refreshes.

**Checkout.** The order service creates an order and calls the payment processor with an idempotency key equal to the order ID. On success: `UPDATE seats SET status='sold', order_id=$o WHERE hold_id=$h AND status='held' AND hold_expires_at > now() - interval '2 minutes'` (a small grace period). If that updates zero rows, the payment is refunded automatically and the user is told.

questions.explanation: Ticketing combines a thundering herd with a strict no-oversell rule. The waiting room turns the herd into a controlled rate, and atomic conditional updates on a per-seat row make holds and sales correct without long-lived locks, with expiry built into the condition so it never depends on a background job. Payment is the slow external step, so the design must handle the case where it succeeds after the hold ran out. Takeaway: put the invariant in a single atomic statement at the source of truth, and treat every other view of availability as a hint.

questions.title: File sync across devices with offline edits
questions.prompt: Design a file sync service for 100M users. Files can be up to 50 GB. Desktop and mobile clients sync a folder across several devices, can edit offline, and can share folders with other users. Uploads should send only what changed, and small edits should reach a user's other devices within a few seconds. Sketch the components and explain how a file is uploaded, how other devices learn about the change, and what happens when two devices edit the same file offline.

keyPoints: Splits files into chunks of a few MB (fixed-size or content-defined), addresses each by a content hash, and uploads only chunks the server does not already have, resumably and directly to object storage (for example with pre-signed URLs)
Keeps metadata (namespaces, file tree, versions as ordered lists of chunk hashes) in a strongly consistent database sharded by namespace, with a per-namespace change journal and cursor
Commits in two phases: chunks first, then a metadata commit that the server verifies references only existing chunks, so a file version never points at missing data
Notifies devices of namespace changes over a long-lived connection (long poll or WebSocket), after which clients pull deltas from their cursor
Detects conflicting edits with optimistic concurrency (each commit names its parent version) and keeps both versions as a conflicted copy instead of silently overwriting
Garbage-collects unreferenced chunks with reference counting or mark-and-sweep after a grace period, and explains that shared folders are separate namespaces mounted into each member's tree
redFlags: Re-uploading the whole file on every change
Storing file contents in the metadata database
Last-writer-wins on concurrent edits with no conflict copy
Clients polling the full file tree to detect changes
rubric.exemplar:
**Upload.** The client watches the folder, splits a changed file into ~4 MB chunks, and hashes each with SHA-256. It asks the metadata service which hashes are missing, uploads only those to object storage via pre-signed URLs (resumable, in parallel), then commits: `commit(namespace, path, parent_version, [hashes])`. The service checks that every hash exists and that `parent_version` is still current, writes the new version and appends an entry to the namespace journal in one transaction.

**Metadata.** Namespaces (a user's root or a shared folder) map to shards in a strongly consistent store. Each namespace has a monotonically increasing journal ID. Shared folders are their own namespace mounted into each member's tree, so a change is written once.

**Notify.** Each device keeps a long-lived connection to a notification service subscribed to its namespaces. On commit, the service pushes "namespace X changed"; the device calls `list_changes(cursor)` and downloads only missing chunks. That gives seconds-level propagation.

**Conflicts.** If a device commits with a stale `parent_version`, the commit is rejected; the client keeps the server version and saves its own as "file (conflicted copy from laptop)." Nothing is silently lost.

**GC.** Chunks are reference-counted from versions; versions expire under the retention policy, and chunks at zero references are deleted after a 30-day grace period.

questions.explanation: File sync separates bulk content from metadata: content-addressed chunks in object storage give deduplication, resumable uploads and delta sync, while a small, strongly consistent metadata store with per-namespace journals gives ordering and cheap change detection. Concurrent offline edits are a product decision, and the safe default is to keep both versions. Takeaway: put large immutable bytes and small mutable metadata in different systems, and make the metadata commit the single point where a change becomes real.

questions.title: Search-box autocomplete under 50 ms
questions.prompt: Design autocomplete for an e-commerce search box. There are 50M searches per day, and the client requests suggestions as the user types, about 8 requests per search. Suggestions are ranked by popularity, must include trending queries within an hour, must never show offensive terms, and need p99 under 50 ms. Sketch the components and explain how suggestions are built, served, and kept fresh.

keyPoints: Estimates load: 50M × 8 = 400M requests/day, about 4,600/s average and roughly 15k to 25k/s at peak, and reduces it with client debouncing and caching

Builds suggestions offline from query logs in the warehouse: aggregates and scores queries, precomputes the top k completions per prefix, and publishes a versioned index (trie, FST or prefix-to-top-k map)
Serves from memory on stateless, replicated nodes loaded with the latest snapshot, bounded in size (prefix length cap, top 10 per prefix), and caches short, hot prefixes at the CDN or edge
Handles trending with a streaming job over recent queries that maintains a small delta layer merged with the base results at read time
Filters offensive terms with a blocklist applied at build time and again at serve time so new entries take effect without a rebuild
Keeps personalization off the critical path: re-rank a small candidate set using recent user history, with a fallback to global results
redFlags: A `LIKE 'prefix%'` query against the product database on each keystroke
Rebuilding the whole index synchronously as each query comes in
No debounce, so every keystroke costs a request
Applying the blocklist only at build time
rubric.exemplar:
**Load.** 400M requests/day is about 4,600/s average, maybe 20k/s at peak. Clients debounce by about 100 ms and cache results per prefix for the session, which cuts real traffic substantially.

**Build.** An hourly job over query logs in the warehouse normalizes queries, scores them (recency-weighted count plus conversion rate), drops blocked terms, and computes the top 10 completions for every prefix up to 20 characters. It writes a versioned snapshot to object storage.

**Serve.** Suggestion servers load the snapshot into an in-memory map (prefix to top 10) and swap atomically on a new version; they are stateless and replicated behind a load balancer, so lookups are a hash read and p99 is a few milliseconds. One- and two-character prefixes, the hottest, are cacheable at the CDN for a minute.

**Trending.** A streaming job counts queries over a sliding hour and pushes a small delta (prefix to trending completions) to the servers every minute; the server merges delta and base by score.

**Safety.** The blocklist lives in a config store and is applied again at serve time, so adding a term takes effect within a minute.

**Personalization.** Optional: re-rank the top 20 candidates with the user's recent categories, with a 10 ms budget and fallback to global order.

questions.explanation: Typeahead works because almost all of the work can be precomputed: the number of useful prefixes is bounded, so top-k per prefix fits in memory and serving becomes a lookup. Freshness comes from layering a small streaming delta over a periodic batch build, and safety needs a serve-time filter because batch builds are slow to react. Takeaway: when the read latency budget is tiny, move the computation offline and keep the serving path a memory lookup.
